thread.subject: Re: RE: made you something
thread.body_text:
Hey Kyle, this is interesting - I definitely like the way it creates a system. I will say, I'm doing a lot of Springs Fireplace writing with my own GPT and I think I could make this playbook more authentic by feeding existing content into it. In addition, I can tell these photos are AI, and I don't love that. All that being said, I would still like to learn how your product works, and I have set up some time for next week. I simply wanted to offer this feedback so you understand my thinking before our call.  

 Thanks, 
 Lauren

this is exactly the kind of feedback I want, thank you Lauren.
 

 you're right that you can tell on the photos, and that one's on the inputs. those mockups were built from whatever I could pull off your site, so the model was guessing at your bottles, your labels, your peppers. when we build creative for a brand we're actually running, we start from their real product photography and shoot library, and the output stops reading as generated. same tools, completely different starting point.
 

 and on the playbook, no argument. yours was written from the outside in, site and reviews only. feeding your own content into it is the right instinct.
 

 the part I'd focus on next week is the layer above the creative, how the account is structured, what gets tested in what order, and how you know which angle is working before you spend real money on it. that's the piece a GPT can't do for you.
 

 see you next week.

 - Kyle

copy.tldr: Springs Fireplace is a premium seed-to-bottle hot sauce brand with an Oprah's Favorite Things 2025 badge and no ads running yet, so this call is about starting clean from their bestseller Tesuque, not fixing a broken account.

deep_dive.what_they_are: A small premium condiment brand that grows rare peppers on their own farm in East Hampton and nearby New York and New Jersey partners, then bottles hot sauce, salsa, and pepper flakes seed-to-bottle. They were selected as one of Oprah's Favorite Things 2025.
deep_dive.what_they_sell: 12 products from $8 to $35. Hot sauces (Tesuque, Aji Peach, Aji Mango), salsa (Salsa Roja), pepper flakes (Gochugaru, Aleppo, Espelette, Aji Limon), rare peppers (Charapita), and gift sets (The Duo, The Trifecta, Aji Lovers). Median price is $14, which I am using as the stand-in for their average order value since we cannot see their real numbers.
deep_dive.positioning: Premium, provenance-first artisan condiments for people who want flavor and heritage over generic store-bought heat. The pitch is clean ingredients, rare peppers with a real story, and heat that lifts flavor rather than burning.
deep_dive.who_buys: Flavor-curious home cooks and food lovers who care about where food comes from, want clean ingredients like no added sugar and no preservatives, and will pay more for a hot sauce with a story.
strengths: Real credibility markers most food brands never get. Oprah's Favorite Things 2025, a Scovie Award for Tesuque and Salsa Roja, and an International Flave Award for Aji Peach.
A clear premium story that is easy to build ads around. Own farm, rare peppers, glass not plastic, clean ingredients.
gaps: No reviews visible anywhere on the site, so there is no social proof for a cold shopper to lean on.
No Meta ads found running, so they are starting from zero. There is no past data, no proven audience, and no warm pixel to build from.

game_plan.headline: Start from their award-winning bestseller Tesuque, prove one ad can sell cold, then widen and add a second product only after something works.

phases.goal: Prove that paid ads can sell to people who have never heard of the brand. Find one ad and one product that work.
campaigns: One simple sales campaign targeting cold audiences, built around Tesuque
A basic retargeting campaign so people who visit but do not buy see the brand again
lead_products: Tesuque - I would lead with this. Their own site calls it their best-selling hot sauce, and it is a 2025 Scovie Award winner. At $14 it sits right at their median price, and it is described as an everyday condiment, which means repeat use and a wider audience than a niche fiery sauce.
phases.creative: Start from the three ads in the Scroll-Stopper Sheet we already sent. Go live first with the ad that leads on Tesuque and the award, because it pairs their strongest product with proof a stranger will trust. Lauren flagged the mockup images read as AI, so before launch we swap in their real product photography and shoot library. Same angles, real bottles.
phases.budget: Around $30 to $50 a day to start.
phases.what_success_looks_like: We can see which ad and which audience get the cheapest clicks and the first sales. We are not chasing scale yet, just a signal that something works.

phases.goal: Put more money behind whatever won in month one and widen the audience.
campaigns: Scale the winning ad and audience with a higher daily budget
Test two or three new audiences that look like the early buyers
Introduce the gift-set angle (The Duo) to lift order value
lead_products: The Duo - Tesuque plus Aji Peach at $26. Both are award winners, and a set nearly doubles the order value versus a single bottle. Natural next step once the single sauce is proven.
phases.creative: Refresh the winning ad with two or three new versions so it does not go stale. Lean into the award badges and the clean-ingredient story that we know matches their voice.
phases.budget: Step up toward $75 to $100 a day, but only on what is already working.
phases.what_success_looks_like: The winning ad holds up at higher spend, and the gift-set angle starts pulling a higher average order value.

phases.goal: Scale the proven setup and add a second hero product.
campaigns: Push spend on the proven winners
Launch a second product line as its own hero
Broaden retargeting to include gift buyers heading into the holiday season
lead_products: Salsa Roja - a 2025 Scovie Award winner and, per their site, it was out of stock and came back, which usually means demand. A salsa reaches a slightly different buyer than a hot sauce, which widens the top of the funnel.
Aji Peach - International Flave Award winner, sits at $14, and anchors The Duo, so it doubles as a set-seller.
phases.creative: Fresh ads for the second product built on the same proven structure. Start layering in gift-set messaging since 90 days out lands near holiday buying.
phases.budget: Scale spend in step with return. No fixed ceiling. We only spend more where the money keeps coming back.
phases.what_success_looks_like: Two products selling from ads, a stable return we can push, and a gift angle ready for the holidays.

estimates.label: Starting budget
estimates.basis: enough to get roughly 30 to 40 clicks a day at typical costs in this food and condiment category, which is the floor for learning which ad and audience work before spending more

estimates.label: Average order value stand-in
estimates.basis: the median price across their 12 products, used because we have no access to their Shopify. A single bottle is $14, but sets like The Duo at $26 and The Trifecta at $33 could lift this once we push them

estimates.label: Revenue we would aim to add
estimates.value: We would not put a dollar figure on this yet
estimates.basis: with no ad history, no reviews on site, and no view of their real order value or margin, any revenue number would be a guess. Once we know their true average order value and what their margin allows, we can set a real target

assumptions: Tesuque really is their bestseller, based on their own site calling it best-selling. If it is not, we lead with whichever product actually sells most.
Their real average order value is close to the $14 median. If most orders are single $8 flake jars, the math gets tight and we push sets harder.
They have real product photography we can use, since Lauren does not want AI images.
Their margin on a $14 sauce is healthy enough to carry paid ads. We confirm this on the call.
Checkout and shipping work fine. The shipping policy page looked empty, so we should confirm shipping is actually set up.

questions.question: Are you running any paid ads right now, on Meta or anywhere else, and have you ever?
questions.listening_for: We found no ads running. If they never have, this is a true from-zero build and we set slow expectations. If they tried and stopped, find out what happened and why.

questions.question: Who handles your marketing today, you or someone on the team?
questions.listening_for: Lauren mentioned doing a lot of the brand writing herself with a GPT. Confirm whether she is a solo owner wearing every hat or has help. This tells us how hands-on we need to be.

questions.question: When you sell a $14 bottle, roughly how much of that is left after the product and packaging cost?
questions.listening_for: This is the make-or-break number. At a $14 order, ads only work if the margin is strong. If margin is thin, we must push sets from day one.

questions.question: What does a typical order look like, one bottle or a few?
questions.listening_for: Tells us if the real average order value is near $14 or higher. Higher orders give ads much more room to work.

questions.question: What would make this a clear win for you in 90 days?
questions.listening_for: Whether she wants sales, brand awareness off the Oprah moment, or retail-store demand. It changes what we optimize for.

questions.question: You have big awards, Oprah, Scovie, Flave, but I do not see any customer reviews on your site. Are you collecting them anywhere?
questions.listening_for: No reviews on site is the biggest gap for cold ads. If she has reviews sitting in email or Shopify, we can surface them fast. If she has none at all, we lean harder on the awards as proof.

questions.question: When someone new lands on your product page, what usually gets them to buy, the story, the awards, or the ingredients?
questions.listening_for: Tells us which angle to lead the ad with. If she does not know, that itself says we need to test it.

questions.question: Where do most of your sales come from today, your site, stores, markets, or word of mouth?
questions.listening_for: If they are mostly wholesale or farmers markets, the website may not be built to convert cold traffic, which we would need to fix before spending.

questions.question: Is your checkout and shipping fully set up and tested? Your shipping policy page looked empty when I checked.
questions.listening_for: If shipping is not configured, ads would send people into a broken buying flow. This has to be right before we spend a dollar.

questions.question: Do you have real product photos and any video of the bottles or the farm we can use?
questions.listening_for: Lauren does not want AI images. We need real assets. Farm and pepper footage would be gold for the provenance story.

questions.question: After the Oprah feature, did you notice people searching your name or the specific peppers, like Gochugaru or Espelette?
questions.listening_for: These are named peppers people already search for by name. That is a real opening for Google search ads to catch buyers who already want the product. Worth raising honestly here.

questions.question: Are you showing up when someone searches your brand name or your award-winning sauces?
questions.listening_for: If competitors or resellers are bidding on their name after the Oprah bump, a small branded search campaign protects easy sales. Only raise if she confirms search interest.

objections.objection: I can tell your mockups were AI and I do not love that.
objections.answer: You are right, and that is on the inputs. Those were built from whatever I could pull off your site, so the images were guessing at your bottles and labels. When we run ads for you for real, we start from your own product photos and farm footage, so nothing reads as generated. Same angles, real bottles.

objections.objection: I already write my brand voice with my own GPT and I can make the playbook more authentic myself.
objections.answer: That instinct is right, and feeding your own content in makes it better. The part that a GPT cannot do is the layer above the words, how the account is built, what ad we test first, and how you know which angle is working before you spend real money. That is what next week is about.

objections.objection: I have never run ads. Is my brand even ready?
objections.answer: That is actually a clean starting point, no bad habits to undo. You already have the hardest part, real proof most brands never get, with Oprah and two awards. We start small, prove one ad on Tesuque can sell to strangers, then only spend more once something works.

objections.objection: My bottles are only $14, can ads even pay for themselves?
objections.answer: Fair question, and it is why we do not just push single bottles. We lead with Tesuque to get the sale, then move buyers toward sets like The Duo at $26, which lifts the order value. First we confirm your margin, then we build the plan around what the math can actually carry.

red_flags.flag: No reviews visible anywhere on the site.
red_flags.why_it_matters: Cold shoppers trust other buyers. Without reviews we have to carry the whole ad on awards alone, which is harder. We should find and surface reviews before or right as we launch.

red_flags.flag: Average order value stand-in is only about $14.
red_flags.why_it_matters: A single low-priced bottle leaves little room to pay for ads and still profit. If their real order value and margin are thin, the plan has to push sets from the start.
If shipping is not fully set up, ads would send buyers into a broken checkout and waste spend. Confirm it works before launching.

red_flags.flag: Several sauces need refrigeration after opening and note being out of stock.
red_flags.why_it_matters: Perishable, small-batch products can hit stock limits fast. Scaling ads on something that sells out burns money and frustrates buyers. We need to confirm stock can keep up before we push spend.

other_channel_openings: Google search ads on their named peppers. Terms like Gochugaru, Espelette, and Aleppo are things people already search for by name, so there is real existing demand to catch.
Branded search protection. After the Oprah's Favorite Things feature, people are likely searching the brand name directly, and a small campaign makes sure Springs Fireplace shows up first.
